t: LeetCode 2248 - Intersection of Multiple Arrays: Frequency Counting vs Set Intersection
o: **Understanding the problem.** Every row of `nums` is a set - values are distinct within a row - and we want the values present in ALL rows, sorted ascending. Example 1 keeps only 3 and 4; example 2 has no overlap at all, yielding an empty list. The input is tiny (at most 1000 total entries, values bounded by 1000), so both a frequency sweep and successive set intersections run instantly. Because values repeat only ACROSS rows, "global frequency equals the number of rows" is a precise membership test.
k: Values are unique per row, so a value lies in every row iff its global count equals `nums.length`.
Values are bounded by 1000 - a flat count array beats hashing and yields sorted output by scanning ascending.
Intersecting sets pairwise also works; intersecting with smaller rows first shrinks candidates fastest.

a.i: Tally each value across all rows, then collect values whose tally matches the row count. Scanning candidate values 1..1000 in ascending order produces the required sorted output for free, with no final sort.
s: Count occurrences of every value across all rows.
For `v` from 1 to 1000, emit `v` when its count equals `nums.length`.
a.t: O(N + V) - N total entries tallied plus a sweep over the V = 1000 possible values.

a.i: Start from the first row as a set and repeatedly intersect with each subsequent row, keeping only survivors. The candidate set can only shrink, which often finishes faster in practice despite needing a final sort.
s: For each later row, keep exactly the elements that also appear in that row.
Sort the surviving set ascending and return it.
a.t: O(N + R log R) - linear intersection work plus sorting the R survivors.

w: Both approaches are interview-safe; counting showcases exploiting bounded values while sets generalize to arbitrary ranges. Pitfalls: forgetting the required ascending order and misapplying multiset logic - rows are duplicate-free, which is what makes counting sound. Follow-ups: rows too large for memory (intersect incrementally against the current smallest set), or reporting how many rows contain each common element.
